cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: Conduction: heat transfer through direct contact — e.g. pan on hob transferring heat to food through the metal. Best for: frying, sautéing, griddling.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: Convection: heat transfer through fluid (liquid or air) movement — hot fluid rises, cool fluid sinks, creating currents. Best for: baking (hot air), boiling/simmering (hot water), roasting.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: Radiation: heat transfer through electromagnetic waves without needing a medium — e.g. grilling, toasting. The heat source emits infrared radiation that is absorbed by the food surface.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: Microwave cooking: microwaves (electromagnetic waves) cause water molecules in food to vibrate rapidly, generating heat through friction. Microwaves penetrate about 4cm, so thick foods cook from outside in. Not suitable for pastry or crispy textures.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: Baking: convection (hot air) + conduction (through baking tray). Temperature typically 180-220°C. Produces browning (Maillard reaction), rising (gas expansion, steam), and setting (protein coagulation, starch gelatinisation).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: Boiling: convection (hot water) at 100°C. Nutrients (especially water-soluble vitamins) leach into water. Use minimal water and cook for shortest time to preserve nutrients.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: Steaming: convection (steam) — food doesn't touch water so fewer nutrients lost. Healthier cooking method retaining flavour, colour, and texture. Temperature 100°C but steam transfers heat efficiently.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: Frying: shallow (conduction from pan + convection of hot fat), deep (convection — food fully immersed in fat at 160-180°C), stir-fry (conduction — very hot wok, quick cooking). High fat content if deep-fried.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: Roasting: radiation (from oven walls) + convection (hot air) + conduction (through roasting tin). Dry heat method producing browning and caramelisation. Often uses fat/oil to aid heat transfer and flavour.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: Grilling: radiation from heat source above or below. Quickly cooks surface, creating browning and flavour through Maillard reaction. Healthier than frying as fat drains away.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: Choosing cooking methods: consider the food type (tough meats need slow moist cooking, delicate fish needs gentle heat), nutritional impact (retain vitamins), desired texture, time available, and health considerations.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods
cards.back: The Maillard reaction: a chemical reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars at temperatures above 140°C, producing browning and complex flavour compounds. Essential for the flavour of grilled meat, baked bread, and roasted coffee.

cards.front: What should you know about food preparation & nutrition exam tips — heat transfer & cooking methods?
cards.back: 1. For Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods questions, show every step of your working clearly — method marks count even if the final answer is wrong 2. Check your answer makes sense in context (estimation, units, reasonableness) 3. Use correct mathematical notation and state formulae before substituting values 4. If a Heat Transfer & Cooking Methods question asks you to 'prove' or 'show', write a logical chain of reasoning with a conclusion line 5. For problem-solving, identify the topic first, then recall the relevant method
